title: Life in the Spirit: No Condemnation, No Separation
summary: Paul declares that there is no condemnation for those in Christ, because God has done in his Son what the law could not do, and the Spirit now gives life and leads believers as God's adopted children. Present suffering, shared by a groaning creation, is set against the glory to come, and the Spirit prays within believers' weakness. The chapter ends in a series of questions and a confident claim that nothing in all creation can separate God's people from his love in Christ.
story: Romans 7 ended with a cry of frustration, a person who delights in God's law yet finds another law at work in the body, and a sudden word of thanks to God through Jesus Christ. Chapter 8 explains that thanks. It answers the problem of chapters 5 to 7 (sin, death, and a law that could not give life) by introducing the Holy Spirit, who is mentioned only a handful of times in chapters 1 to 7 and about twenty times here. The chapter also completes the argument that began in 5:1, that those justified by faith have peace with God and a sure hope of glory. It closes the first great movement of the letter. After it, Paul will turn in chapters 9 to 11 to the question its confident ending raises: if God's promises cannot fail, what about Israel?
historical:
Paul wrote Romans most likely from Corinth around AD 57, near the end of his third missionary campaign, to believers in Rome he had not yet visited. The church there met in several households and included both Jews and Gentiles. The Roman historian Suetonius reports that the emperor Claudius expelled Jews from Rome because of disturbances, an event Acts 18:2 also mentions and which is usually dated around AD 49; after Claudius died in AD 54 many Jews, Jewish believers among them, returned under Nero. That history of displacement probably shaped tensions between Jewish and Gentile believers, which Paul addresses directly in chapters 14 and 15.

The list of hardships in 8:35 (trouble, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, danger, and sword) is not abstract. Paul had already been beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked, and hungry, as he recounts in 2 Corinthians 11. The believers in Rome would later suffer under Nero, who blamed Christians for the great fire of AD 64. Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, a lament of Israel suffering even though it had not forgotten God, and applies it to the church's present life.
cultural:
Paul's language of adoption would have landed with force in Rome. Roman law allowed a man to adopt a son, often an adult, to carry on his name and inherit his estate, and the adopted son received the full legal standing of a natural heir. The practice reached the top of Roman society: Octavian, who became Augustus, was adopted in the will of Julius Caesar, and Nero himself was adopted by Claudius in AD 50. Paul also draws on Israel's own story, since Israel was called God's son and was freed from slavery in Egypt. When he says believers have received not a spirit of slavery but the Spirit of adoption, both backgrounds are in view.

The cry "Abba" is Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke, and means "Father". Paul keeps the Aramaic word even when writing in Greek to a Roman church, most likely because it came from Jesus' own prayer (Mark 14:36) and had passed into the worship of Greek-speaking believers. The word "firstfruits" comes from Israel's harvest festivals, where the first part of the crop was offered to God as a pledge that the rest of the harvest would follow. The image of creation groaning in childbirth draws on a common Jewish picture of the suffering that would come before the new age, the birth pains of the Messiah's era.
literary: Romans 8 is argument that rises toward praise. It opens with "no condemnation" (verse 1) and ends with no separation (verses 38-39), framing the whole chapter in assurance. Verses 1 to 17 contrast two ways of existing, according to the flesh and according to the Spirit, in a series of balanced statements. Verses 18 to 30 move from the individual to the whole creation and are held together by the word "groan", used of creation (verse 22), of believers (verse 23), and of the Spirit's own intercession (verse 26). Verses 29 and 30 form a chain in which each link leads to the next, foreknew, predestined, called, justified, glorified, with the last verb put in the past tense as though already done. Verses 31 to 39 are a courtroom scene built from rhetorical questions (who is against us, who will bring a charge, who condemns, who will separate), each answered by what God has done in Christ.

outline.t: No condemnation: God did what the law could not
Flesh and Spirit: two minds, two ends
The Spirit of adoption: children and heirs
Present suffering, a groaning creation, and future glory
The Spirit's prayer and God's unbroken purpose
Nothing can separate us from the love of God

doctrines.note: The Spirit is the dominant theme of the chapter. He gives life, dwells in believers, leads them, assures them they are God's children, and prays for them in their weakness. Paul calls him both the Spirit of God and the Spirit of Christ (verse 9), and the chapter's movement among Father, Son, and Spirit is one of the texts the church drew on in confessing the Trinity.

Salvation here has a past, present, and future. There is no condemnation now, believers are being led by the Spirit and putting sin to death, and they wait for the redemption of their bodies. Verse 24 says we were saved in hope, which holds all three together.

Christian hope in this chapter is not only for souls but for bodies and for the whole creation, which will be set free from its bondage to decay. Hope is defined as waiting patiently for what cannot yet be seen.

Verses 28 to 30 describe God's purpose running from foreknowledge to glory without a break, as the ground of believers' security. How foreknowledge and predestination relate to human faith is debated, and Paul takes up election more fully in chapter 9.

words.note: Katakrima, condemnation, meaning the sentence passed after a verdict and the penalty that follows. The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in Romans (5:16, 5:18, and here). Paul had used it for the condemnation that came through Adam; now he says that for those in Christ there is none, because God has "condemned sin in the flesh" (verse 3) in the death of his Son.

Huiothesia, adoption as sons, literally the placing as a son. The word was a legal term in the Greek and Roman world and is used in the New Testament only by Paul. It describes a present status (verse 15) and a future completion (verse 23), the redemption of the body. Paul uses it in 9:4 for Israel as well, so believers are joined to a sonship God first gave his people.

Stenazo, to groan or sigh under pressure. Believers groan inwardly as they wait (verse 23), and the related words describe creation groaning together (verse 22) and the Spirit's groans too deep for words (verse 26). Paul does not treat groaning as a failure of faith. It is the sound of people who have tasted the new creation and are not yet in it.

Pneuma, spirit, breath, wind. It appears twenty-one times in this chapter, more than in any other chapter of Paul's letters. Most uses refer to the Holy Spirit, but some, such as "our spirit" in verse 16, refer to the human spirit, and translators must decide case by case, which is why some English versions capitalize differently.

christ: The chapter shows Christ as the one through whom God dealt with sin decisively. God sent his own Son "in the likeness of sinful man, as an offering for sin" (verse 3): truly human, yet not himself sinful, bearing the condemnation that sin deserved. The Spirit who lives in believers is the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of the God who raised Jesus from the dead, so Christ's resurrection is the pattern and pledge of theirs (verse 11). Believers are co-heirs with Christ, sharing his sufferings now and his glory later, and they are being conformed to his image so that he is "the firstborn among many brothers" (verse 29). The echo of Genesis 22 is widely noticed in verse 32: God "did not spare His own Son", as Abraham did not withhold Isaac, though here the Son is actually given up. Christ now intercedes at God's right hand (verse 34), and it is his love, and God's love in him, from which nothing can separate his people.

hard.q: Does Romans 8:28 mean that everything that happens is good?
hard.a:
Verse 28 is often quoted as if it said that every event is good in itself or that believers will always see a happy outcome. The text says something both more modest and more solid: God works all things together for the good of those who love him. The "all things" in context include the sufferings just listed (verse 18), the groaning of creation, and the trouble, famine, and sword of verse 35. Paul doesn't call those things good. He says they cannot defeat God's purpose. The good is defined in the next verse as being conformed to the image of his Son, which is more than comfort or success.

Interpreters differ on some details. Some manuscripts name God as the subject who works, while others make all things the subject that work together, and translations vary accordingly, though the sense of God's active purpose is present either way. Readers also differ on how verses 29 and 30 relate God's foreknowledge to human faith. Reformed readers take foreknowledge as God's prior choosing love; Arminian readers take it as God's foreknowledge of those who would believe. Both agree that the verse is a promise of God's faithfulness to his people in suffering, not a denial that suffering is real or evil.

questions: Paul says there is "now no condemnation" for those in Christ. Where do you still live as if the verdict on you were undecided?
The chapter treats groaning, for ourselves and for the created world, as part of faithful waiting. What would change if you let yourself groan honestly before God?
Which item in Paul's list in verses 35 to 39 feels most able to separate you from God's love, and what does the chapter say to it?
